content: Aerosinusitis, also known as barosinusitis, sinus squeeze, or sinus barotrauma, is a condition characterized by painful inflammation and sometimes bleeding of the mucosal lining of the paranasal sinuses, most commonly the frontal sinuses. Sinus barotrauma often occurs in individuals with a preceding upper respiratory tract infection or allergic condition. Affected individuals typically experience a sudden, sharp facial pain or headache during descent, which intensifies as the aircraft approaches ground level. This can result in the accumulation of fluid or blood within the sinus cavity. The most common symptom of sinus barotrauma is localized pain in the frontal region. Less frequently, pain may radiate to the temporal, occipital, or retrobulbar areas. In some cases, epistaxis (nosebleeds) or serosanguineous nasal discharge may occur. Neurological symptoms can also arise, particularly involving the fifth cranial nerve, with the infraorbital nerve being most commonly affected. Fighter pilots, who experience the most extreme barometric changes, are particularly susceptible, although commercial aviation has also contributed to the prevalence of the condition. Two types of acute barotrauma are recognized: squeeze and reverse squeeze. During ascent, the air within the sinuses expands, while during descent, it contracts. Campbell and Weissman classified sinus barotrauma into three grades based on symptom severity. Grade I involves mild, transient sinus discomfort without radiographic changes. Grade II is characterized by severe pain lasting up to 24 hours, with some mucosal thickening visible on X-ray. Grade III presents with severe pain persisting for more than 24 hours, accompanied by significant mucosal thickening or opacification on X-ray, and may include epistaxis or subsequent sinusitis. The frontal sinuses are most commonly affected, likely due to the relatively long and narrow nasofrontal duct that connects the frontal sinuses to the nasal cavity. Barotrauma involving the maxillary, ethmoidal, or sphenoidal sinuses is less common and typically occurs when the ostia are obstructed, often due to an acute upper respiratory tract infection. While high-performance aircraft with lower pressurized cabins are more likely to cause severe cases, even commercial flights can result in significant barotrauma. Mild cases of sinus barotrauma are effectively managed with topical decongestants and analgesics. However, severe or treatment-resistant cases may require functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) to restore sinus drainage and ventilation. This approach has demonstrated favorable outcomes, particularly in aviators with recurrent sinus barotrauma. Computer-aided endoscopic surgery has been particularly effective in addressing sphenoidal sinus involvement, where endoscopic examination often reveals mucosal petechiae and hematomas.
